extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, patent and trademark attorneys, and in-house counsel handling prosecution and litigation in Mexico and Paraguay
extracted.subtask_description: Country practice guide describing prosecution and enforcement procedures, remedies, timelines, evidentiary rules, invalidity/revocation grounds, and patentability issues for patents and trademarks in Mexico (and a Paraguay patents excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation delay (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial stage before the IMPI of a patent infringement action usually takes 18 to 20 months; once IMPI issues a decision, two further stages of appeals before courts lasting no less than three further years are expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for multi-year proceedings when assessing enforcement strategy and timing for damages claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of Limitations and limits on damage claims (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statute of limitations for infringement generally, however there is a two-year limitation period to pursue a civil action for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil law (suppletory) timing to claim damages must be considered when deciding when to file infringement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions and interim reliefs (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: IMPI can order an alleged infringer to cease infringing activities, withdraw products from the marketplace and conduct seizures; proceedings are inaudita altera pars (no formal hearing) and followed in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must file an infringement claim within twenty business days after measures are notified. Preliminary injunctions become permanent only once the infringement action is resolved. Plaintiff does not have to show likelihood of success in the merits to obtain injunctions; marking is a condition to request preliminary injunctions and award monetary damages (can be substituted by nationwide publications). Plaintiff must post a reasonable bond; defendant may lift measures by posting a counter-bond equal to plaintiff's bond plus 40%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex-parte remedies / criminal actions (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal actions for patent infringement are only available for re-offense cases — infringement after a final IMPI decision declaring the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-offense may be pursued ex-officio or ex-parte through the Federal District Attorney Office (PGR) and punished with up to 6 years imprisonment and a fine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil remedies — damages and lost profits (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary relief obtainable from courts is actual losses and lost profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages require clear and convincing evidence showing direct cause-effect (e.g., lost sales due to infringing product). Civil actions are filed once an administrative action is final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonds (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no established guidelines related to bonds; practice depends on criteria under which plaintiff posted bonds and defendant sought lifting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect case-by-case treatment; prepare for posting a reasonable bond to obtain preliminary measures and anticipate counter-bond strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation procedures — invalidity action (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant can file an invalidity action as a counterclaim with the response to the infringement action, or an independent invalidity action (if not filed with the response it will be decided separately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IP law establishes several grounds for invalidation (see separate grounds entries). Invalidity decisions are difficult to obtain and require proof that the invalidity cause occurred; conclusive evidence is usually necessary and IMPI may render a technical report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for patent invalidity (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IP law establishes grounds such as: (1) granted in contravention of requirements and conditions; (2) granted contravening law provisions in force when granted; (3) application abandoned while prosecuted; (4) granted by error or to someone not entitled; (5) other general causes based on law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions under (1) and (2) may be filed at any time; (3) and (4) only within five years from the publication effective date. Prepare conclusive evidence to meet standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery / pre-trial procedures (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery/pre-trial discovery as in common law is not applicable to Mexico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect broad pre-trial discovery; rely on administrative inspection powers and evidence rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support — admissible evidence and common forms (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may file any kind of evidence except confessional and testimonial evidence unless included with an affidavit, and evidence contrary to morality and the law. Common evidence includes inspection visits to infringer premises and expert witness testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspection visits are conducted by IMPI inspectors typically at service of notice and/or when imposing preliminary injunctions. Use technical experts to analyze infringing devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Mexican law the burden of proof lies with the person who brings an action; for process patents the burden may shift to defendant if some requirements are fulfilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prepare to prove infringement; check whether burden-shifting applies in process patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert evidence (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert evidence is not required by law but is advisable in most cases because inventions often involve technical issues only clarifiable by an expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer expert reports to clarify technical aspects; IMPI may consider technical reports from its Patent Department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witnesses (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: IMPI has rejected testimonial evidence unless included with an affidavit; affidavits are not considered a primary source; Mexican law does not allow live testimony or cross-examination of witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan evidence strategy without expectation of live witness examination before IMPI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate practice (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review recourse before IMPI (optional) is resolved by the administrative superior that issued the refusal; appeals are available to the Specialized IP Court within the Federal Court of Administrative Affairs (FCA), and final appeals to the Federal Circuit Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review recourse is advisable when denial is due to clear mistakes of IMPI (e.g., mistyped or misfiled documents); for substantive refusals, direct appeal to FCA/Federal Circuit may be appropriate. Appeals are decided on written arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and alternative dispute resolution (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlement is very unusual before decision because contingency and recovery depend on a final decision; the IP Law does foresee settlement possibilities but incentives are limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect low settlement likelihood during long administrative and appellate processes; consider ADR only where practical incentives exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee shifting / attorney fees (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney fees do not apply through the whole administrative proceeding; in civil actions for damages they are hard to obtain and discretionary to the judge; civil laws recognize attorney fees but do not expressly state how judges should apply them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for attorney fees; do not rely on fee-shifting as a routine remedy in Mexico.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is general regulation about personal liability, but so far there have been no precedents in Mexico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal liability claims are theoretically available but untested; counsel should monitor jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust issues (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no precedent in Mexico of antitrust, unfair competition or business-related tort actions brought against patentees for the use of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts generally consider the use of a state-given right cannot constitute a violation in these areas; antitrust risk from exercise of patent rights appears low based on available precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of trademarks (prosecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominative, figurative, combined and three-dimensional signs; in accordance with the IP Law, all visible signs can be protected provided they are sufficiently distinctive and able to identify the products or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design registrations and three-dimensional marks are possible but must be distinctive; audible, olfactory and taste perceptions cannot be protected in Mexico.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unregistrable marks (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Olfactory, position, tactile and sound trademarks cannot be protected in Mexico. Marks that are identical or confusingly similar to registered or pending marks for same/similar products, descriptive and generic marks, geographic indications and names of places characterized by manufacture are also not registrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess registrability for distinctiveness and absence of confusing similarity; avoid descriptive/generic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-dimensional and functional shapes (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-dimensional forms of common usage or those imposed by nature or industrial function are not registrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shapes dictated by function or common usage are vulnerable to refusal or cancellation for lack of distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Famous and well-known marks criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark shall be considered famous in Mexico when the majority of consumers are aware of the trademark. A mark is 'well known' when a given sector of the public or business circles is aware of it as a result of business activities or promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of consumer awareness, market penetration and promotion supports famous/well-known status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness and confusing similarity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks must not be visually, phonetically and ideologically similar to previously registered marks or pending applications applied to the same or similar products or services; marks should be analyzed as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess similarity across appearance, sound and meaning; consider the overall impression rather than isolated elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application formalities (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Required information includes applicant's full name and street address, identification of the trademark, type of trademark, description of goods/services, use in commerce in Mexico (intent-to-use allowed), factory/business address if used in Mexico, and convention priority details if claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full dates of first use where applicable and detailed goods/services descriptions to reduce objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection provided by pending applications (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending trademark applications provide priority rights over future applicants who later intend to register a similar trademark covering similar goods or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication and timely filing secure priority; include accurate priority claim information when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution delays (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: If duly filed and no objections/prior references are cited, registration may be granted within 5–6 months; if formalities, requirements or objections are cited, prosecution may last between 12 and 18 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect longer prosecution where examiners raise absolute or relative grounds; plan timelines accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition system (trademarks) — Reform (2016)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Reform (effective Aug 30, 2016) new applications will be published for opposition within 10 working days of filing; opponents have a non-extendable one month from publication to file opposition with documentation; IMPI will publish oppositions within 10 working days; owners have one month to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition does not suspend prosecution; IMPI may optionally consider opponent/applicant arguments; post-registration invalidation grounds remain available. Prepare swift opposition or defensive briefs within tight one-month windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional applications (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional applications are not allowed in Mexico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intent-to-use applications where appropriate; provisional filings (as in some jurisdictions) are not a procedural option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interviews (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews are not expressly regulated by law; usually examiners are willing to hear applicants, but interviews are not binding on examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews as an informal tool to clarify matters, but do not rely on them to secure binding commitments from examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain name registration (process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any individual or legal entity can request domain name registration; check availability at an ICANN-authorized registrar, pay fees and provide administrative, technical and contact information; registrar submits technical info to the Registry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain registration is a separate administrative process — availability and timely registration are key; keep registrar records updated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark infringement — statutory definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts constituting infringement include: I) distributing/placing products on sale or offering services with indication they are protected by a registered trademark when they are not; II) using a trademark confusingly similar to another registered mark for identical/similar products or services; III) using names, signs, symbols, abbreviations or emblems prohibited by law; IV) using combinations of distinctive signs and operating elements/images to induce confusion (unfair competition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims before IMPI begin with a formal written claim; both parties must produce supporting evidence at filing/answer stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the trademark owner or the recorded licensee has standing to enforce trademark rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure ownership or recorded licensee status before initiating proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' / adjudicator expertise (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: IMPI is an administrative agency (not a court of law) with first-instance jurisdiction over trademark infringement; a specialized IP Court at the Federal Court for Administrative Affairs reviews cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect administrative-style proceedings at IMPI and specialized administrative review at FCA; arguments are submitted in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation delay (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial stage before IMPI of trademark infringement usually takes 12 to 18 months; after IMPI decision two further appellate stages before courts lasting at least three further years are expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor long multi-year timelines into enforcement strategy and client expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation venue (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks can be enforced against an infringer only before the IMPI (administrative procedure) in first instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil damages claims are filed in courts only after the administrative action is final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of Limitations and limits on damage claims (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: IMPI’s criterion is that infringement actions must be initiated during the life term of the trademark; civil actions for damages have a two-year limitation period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil claims for damages are subject to a two-year limitation and are filed after administrative decisions become final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions and interim reliefs (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: IMPI can order stop/withdrawal/seizures in inaudita altera pars proceedings; the applicant must file an infringement claim within twenty business days after notification; plaintiff does not have to show likelihood of success; marking is a condition for requesting preliminary injunctions and awarding monetary damages (can be substituted by nationwide publications); plaintiff must post a reasonable bond; defendant may lift measures with a counter-bond equal to plaintiff's plus 40%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply strictly with the 20-business-day filing rule after provisional measures; prepare bonds and marking evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex-parte remedies / criminal actions (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal actions for trademark infringement are only available for re-offense after a final IMPI decision; re-offense is pursued ex-officio or ex-parte through PGR and may be punished with up to 6 years imprisonment and a fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal enforcement is limited and requires prior final administrative finding of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonds (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no established guidelines related to bonds; practice varies based on the criteria under which plaintiff posted bonds and defendant sought lifting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate ad hoc bond amounts; counsel should be prepared to justify bond levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation procedures — invalidity grounds and time limits (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds include: (1) prior use in Mexico/abroad (statute of limitations three years from Gazette publication); (2) registration obtained on false information (five years); (3) existence of senior registration (five years from Gazette publication); (4) registration obtained without authorization of foreign owner/representative (no statute); (5) general cause based on IP law provisions (no statute). Cancellation for non-use available if trademark not used for three consecutive years; registration may be cancelled if mark became generic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different causes carry different limitation periods; plan invalidity or cancellation actions with attention to applicable time bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark invalidity/cancellation procedure (as counterclaim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant in an infringement action can file an invalidity action as a counterclaim when filing the response; if not filed with the response the action will be decided separately from the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider filing invalidity as a counterclaim to consolidate proceedings where strategic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery / pre-trial (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery is not applicable in Mexico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect discovery tools common in common-law jurisdictions; rely on IMPI's evidence-gathering powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: IMPI may obtain necessary evidence; plaintiff may file any kind of evidence except confessional and testimonial evidence unless included with an affidavit; evidence contrary to morality and law is excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof lies with plaintiff. Expert evidence is not required but advisable in specific cases to overcome IMPI criteria; IMPI is the qualified authority to determine registrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witnesses (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: IMPI rejects testimonial evidence unless included with an affidavit; affidavits are not a primary source; Mexican law does not allow live testimony or cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare documentary and expert evidence rather than relying on live witness testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — litigation costs and 40% rule (trademarks and patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may award actual losses and lost profits based on clear and convincing evidence showing direct causation. Additionally, IP Law provides that Civil Courts must impose monetary damages of at least 40% of the commercial value of the infringing products (the '40% rule').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is uncertainty whether the 40% rule is punitive or requires further proof; attorney fees are difficult to obtain and discretionary. Prepare strong evidentiary support for damages and be aware of the statutory minimum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee shifting (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney fees are very hard to get, discretionary to the judge, and civil laws recognize attorney fees without expressly stating how judges should make them applicable; there are no precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume successful fee-shifting; advise clients accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: General regulation exists regarding personal liability but there have been no precedents in Mexico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal liability claims are theoretical and untested — monitor jurisprudence for developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant regulations (Paraguay patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant treaties: Paris Convention (Law No. 300/1994) and TRIPs Agreement (Law No. 444/1994); Patents and Utility Models governed by Law No. 1.630/2000 and Regulatory Decree No. 14.201/2001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference local statutes and international treaty implementations for prosecution and validity analyses in Paraguay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter (Paraguay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to patent are new inventions of products and procedures implying inventive activity and subject to industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability for Paraguayan filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and utility models (Paraguay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design protection governed by Law No. 868/1981 and Regulatory Decree No. 30.007/1982; utility models are patentable under Patent Law No.1.630/2000 and Decree No.14.201/2001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use utility model filings where appropriate; follow local statutes for design protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software patents (Paraguay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims comprising embedded software in a system or in a specific step of a method are usually accepted; 'software per se' is excluded from patentability and protected by copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to tie software functionality to technical apparatus or method steps to improve patentability prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claims (Paraguay pharmaceutical practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds represented by a Markush formula may be admitted if they meet novelty, inventive step and industrial application, present sufficient support in the specification, and properly characterize representative compounds of the various embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sufficient support and representative examples in the specification when filing Markush-style claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological material deposits (Paraguay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological material deposit requirements are referenced though details in the excerpt are incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where biological material is involved, follow applicable deposit and disclosure rules; consult full local statute/regulation.
